slides.narration: A gas fills its container and pushes on every wall, yet we cannot see its molecules. In this part we start from the equation that links pressure, volume and temperature, then picture the gas as a huge number of tiny molecules colliding with the walls, and show that their motion explains both the pressure and the temperature we measure.

slides.heading: The equation of state of an ideal gas
slides.body_md: For an ideal gas the pressure, volume and temperature of a sample are tied together by one relation:
bullets: $n$ is the amount in moles, $N = n N_A$ the number of molecules; $T$ is the **absolute (kelvin) temperature**, $T = t_\text{C} + 273$.
$R = 8.314$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$ and $k_B = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}$ J K$^{-1}$ are related by $R = N_A k_B$.
P in pascal and V in cubic metre give PV in joule; 1 atm = 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa.
An ideal gas obeys this relation at all pressures and temperatures; real gases come close at low pressure and high temperature.

visual.alt: Table of the symbols in the ideal gas equation with their meanings and the values used in this chapter

math: P V = n R T = N k_B T
slides.narration: The ideal gas equation says that pressure times volume equals the number of moles times the gas constant times the temperature. Equivalently it equals the number of molecules times the Boltzmann constant times the temperature. The temperature must be the absolute temperature in kelvin, which is the Celsius value plus two hundred and seventy three. The gas constant equals Avogadro's number times the Boltzmann constant.

slides.heading: The gas laws as special cases
slides.body_md: Hold two of the quantities fixed and the equation reduces to a classical gas law:
bullets: **Boyle:** fixed $n, T$ gives $P V = $ constant: the P–V curves are hyperbolas (isotherms).
**Charles:** fixed $n, P$ gives $V/T = $ constant: a straight line through the origin on the kelvin scale.
**Gay-Lussac:** fixed $n, V$ gives $P/T = $ constant.
**Avogadro:** fixed $P, T$ gives $V \propto n$: equal volumes of any gases hold equal numbers of molecules.
Combined: $\dfrac{P_1 V_1}{T_1} = \dfrac{P_2 V_2}{T_2}$ for a fixed amount of gas.

visual.alt: Pressure-volume curves of one mole of an ideal gas at 250, 300 and 400 kelvin: three hyperbolas, the higher temperature lying farther from the axes; at each volume the pressure is proportional to the temperature
visual.caption: Isotherms: P V = n R T is constant on each curve; hotter curves lie higher.

slides.narration: Fix the amount of gas and the temperature, and the product of pressure and volume stays constant: that is Boyle's law, and the curves on this graph are hyperbolas called isotherms. Fix the pressure and the volume grows in proportion to the kelvin temperature, which is Charles' law. Fix the volume and the pressure is proportional to the kelvin temperature. And at the same pressure and temperature, equal volumes hold equal numbers of molecules.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: helium in a cylinder
slides.body_md: A cylinder of volume $0.05$ m$^3$ holds $4$ mol of helium at $27\,^\circ$C. Find the pressure, taking $R = 8.314$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$.
bullets: $P = \dfrac{n R T}{V} = \dfrac{4 \times 8.314 \times 300}{0.05} = 199536$ Pa.
In round figures $P \approx 2.00 \times 10^{5}$ Pa, about $1.97$ atm.

rows: Pressure P = n R T / V

visual.alt: Table of the data and result for the pressure of helium in a cylinder

slides.narration: Convert to kelvin first: twenty seven plus two hundred and seventy three is three hundred kelvin. Then the pressure is the number of moles times the gas constant times the temperature, divided by the volume. Four times eight point three one four times three hundred, over zero point zero five, gives about two hundred thousand pascals, which is nearly two atmospheres.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: density of air
slides.body_md: Treat dry air (average molar mass $29$ g mol$^{-1}$) as an ideal gas at $1.013 \times 10^5$ Pa and $300$ K. Find its density and the volume of one mole.
bullets: From $P V = n R T$ with $n = m/M$: $\rho = \dfrac{m}{V} = \dfrac{P M}{R T}$.
Molar volume $V_m = \dfrac{R T}{P} = \dfrac{8.314 \times 300}{1.013 \times 10^5} = 0.0246$ m$^3$ $= 24.6$ litre.

visual.alt: Volume-temperature lines of one mole of an ideal gas at 100 and 200 kilopascals: straight lines through the origin on the kelvin scale, the lower pressure having the steeper line
visual.caption: Isobars: V is proportional to T (in kelvin); the lines meet at V = 0 when T = 0 K.

slides.narration: Write the number of moles as mass over molar mass, and the gas equation gives density equal to pressure times molar mass over the gas constant times temperature. For air at one atmosphere and three hundred kelvin that is about one point one eight kilograms per cubic metre. One mole of such a gas occupies about twenty four point six litres.

slides.heading: Real gases and the ideal gas
slides.body_md: The ideal gas is a model; every real gas departs from it somewhere.
bullets: Real molecules have a size and attract one another; the ideal model ignores both.
At low pressure and high temperature the molecules are far apart and the model works well.
At high pressure the molecules' own volume matters; at low temperature attractions matter and the gas liquefies.
The kinetic theory below explains the ideal gas, and tells us what to ignore.

rows: molecules far apart, forces negligible: close to ideal
molecules crowded, their own size matters: departs from ideal
attractions matter, the gas liquefies: departs from ideal

visual.alt: Table of when a real gas behaves like an ideal gas

slides.narration: Real molecules have a size and they attract each other. When the gas is thin and hot, the molecules are far apart and move so fast that these effects hardly matter, so the ideal gas equation works well. Squeeze the gas or cool it, and the departures grow, until the gas finally turns into a liquid.

slides.heading: The kinetic model of an ideal gas
slides.body_md: The pressure is explained by a simple model of the molecules:
bullets: A gas consists of a very large number of identical molecules in constant random motion.
The molecules are so small, compared with their separation, that their own volume is negligible.
There are no forces between molecules except during collisions; between collisions each moves in a straight line.
Collisions, with each other and with the walls, are **elastic**; the gas has no preferred direction.

rows: Many identical molecules in random motion
negligible volume of the molecules themselves
Collisions with walls and with each other are elastic

visual.alt: Table of the assumptions of the kinetic theory of an ideal gas and what each allows

slides.narration: The kinetic model makes five simple assumptions. There are a great many identical molecules moving at random. They are tiny compared with the distances between them. They exert no forces except when they collide. The collisions are elastic, so no kinetic energy is lost. And no direction is special, so on average a third of the squared speed lies along each axis.

slides.heading: Pressure from one collision
slides.body_md: Follow one molecule of mass $m$ in a cube of side $L$.
bullets: It hits the right wall with $+v_x$ and leaves with $-v_x$: momentum change of the molecule $-2 m v_x$, so the wall gets $2 m v_x$.
It crosses the cube and returns in $\dfrac{2L}{v_x}$, so it strikes this wall $\dfrac{v_x}{2L}$ times a second.
Average force from this molecule $= \dfrac{2 m v_x}{2L/v_x} = \dfrac{m v_x^2}{L}$.
Collisions with the other walls and with other molecules do not change this result for the x-direction.

slides.narration: Look at the molecule striking the right hand wall. Its velocity component perpendicular to the wall reverses, so the wall receives twice mass times that component as momentum. The molecule then travels across the cube and back, a distance of two L, before it hits the same wall again. So it delivers a force on average of mass times the component squared, divided by L.

slides.heading: Summing over molecules: P = (1/3) ρ v̄²
slides.body_md: The pressure is the total force on the wall of area $L^2$:
bullets: Because there is no preferred direction, $\overline{v_x^2} = \overline{v_y^2} = \overline{v_z^2}$ and $v^2 = v_x^2 + v_y^2 + v_z^2$.
$\rho = N m / V$ is the mass density; $\overline{v^2}$ is the **mean of the squares** of the speeds.
The pressure is large because N is enormous; it is steady because the collisions are countless.

rows: Time between hits on that wall
Pressure = force ÷ L², sum over N molecules

visual.alt: Table of the steps in deriving the pressure of an ideal gas from molecular collisions

slides.narration: Add up the contribution of all the molecules and divide by the area of the wall. The pressure is the number of molecules times the mass times the average of the squared x component, divided by the volume. With no preferred direction, the average of the squared x component is one third of the average squared speed. So the pressure equals one third of the density times the mean square speed.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: pressure of hydrogen from its speed
slides.body_md: Hydrogen at $0\,^\circ$C has density $0.09$ kg m$^{-3}$ and a mean square speed whose root is $1840$ m s$^{-1}$. Find its pressure.
bullets: $P = \dfrac{1}{3}\rho\,\overline{v^2} = \dfrac{1}{3} \times 0.09 \times 1840^2$.
$P = \dfrac{1}{3} \times 0.09 \times 3385600 = 101568$ Pa $\approx 1.02 \times 10^{5}$ Pa.
This is about one atmosphere, as it should be for hydrogen at 0 °C and ordinary density.

visual.alt: Table of the data and result for the pressure of hydrogen found from its density and rms speed

slides.narration: The pressure is one third of the density times the mean square speed. With a density of point zero nine and a root mean square speed of eighteen hundred and forty metres per second, the squared speed is over three million, and the pressure comes out near one hundred and two thousand pascals, about one atmosphere.

slides.heading: Temperature: mean kinetic energy of translation
slides.body_md: Compare $P V = \tfrac{1}{3} N m \overline{v^2}$ with $P V = N k_B T$:
bullets: The kelvin temperature is a measure of the **mean translational kinetic energy** per molecule; it does not depend on the kind of gas.
$v_\text{rms} \propto \sqrt{T}$ and, at one temperature, $v_\text{rms} \propto 1/\sqrt{M}$: light molecules are fast.
Total translational kinetic energy of n moles: (3/2) n R T.
At T = 0 K the translational motion would cease (in this classical picture).

rows: P V = (2/3) E, with E the total translational kinetic energy
Compare with P V = N k_B T
v_rms = √(3 k_B T / m) = √(3 R T / M)

visual.alt: Table linking pressure, temperature, mean kinetic energy and rms speed

slides.narration: Compare the kinetic result with the gas equation. The average translational kinetic energy of a molecule equals three halves of the Boltzmann constant times the kelvin temperature. So temperature measures the mean kinetic energy, whatever the gas. The root mean square speed is the square root of three k T over the molecular mass, so it grows with the square root of the temperature and falls for heavier molecules.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: speeds of nitrogen and oxygen
slides.body_md: Find the rms speed of nitrogen ($M = 28$ g mol$^{-1}$) and of oxygen ($M = 32$ g mol$^{-1}$) at $300$ K, and the mean translational energy of one molecule.
bullets: $v_\text{rms}(\text{N}_2) = \sqrt{\dfrac{3 \times 8.314 \times 300}{0.028}} = 517$ m s$^{-1}$.
$v_\text{rms}(\text{O}_2) = \sqrt{\dfrac{3 \times 8.314 \times 300}{0.032}} = 484$ m s$^{-1}$, a ratio of $1.07$, equal to $\sqrt{32/28}$.
Mean energy of either molecule $= \tfrac{3}{2} k_B T = 1.5 \times 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \times 300 = 6.21 \times 10^{-21}$ J.

slides.narration: At three hundred kelvin the root mean square speed of nitrogen is about five hundred and seventeen metres per second, and oxygen, which is a little heavier, is about four hundred and eighty three. Their ratio is the square root of thirty two over twenty eight. But the mean kinetic energy per molecule is the same for both, about six point two times ten to the minus twenty one joule.

slides.heading: Mean speed and rms speed
slides.body_md: There are several averages of the molecular speeds; the kinetic theory uses the root of the mean of the squares.
bullets: Mean speed $\bar v = (v_1 + v_2 + \cdots + v_N)/N$; rms speed $v_\text{rms} = \sqrt{(v_1^2 + \cdots + v_N^2)/N}$.
The rms speed is never smaller than the mean speed; they are equal only if all speeds are equal.
The average velocity of the molecules is zero (they move in all directions), but the rms speed is not zero.
Dalton: in a mixture each gas exerts the pressure it would exert alone; the total is the sum of the partial pressures.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: heating a gas
slides.body_md: A gas at $27\,^\circ$C is heated until its rms speed is 1.5 times as large. What is the new temperature in $^\circ$C?
bullets: $v_\text{rms} \propto \sqrt{T}$, so $T_2/T_1 = 1.5^2 = 2.25$.
$t_2 = 675 - 273 = 402\,^\circ$C: not 27 × 1.5, because the scale must be kelvin.

slides.narration: The root mean square speed goes as the square root of the kelvin temperature. A speed one and a half times larger therefore needs a temperature two point two five times larger. Starting from three hundred kelvin, that is six hundred and seventy five kelvin, or four hundred and two degrees Celsius. Using the Celsius scale directly would give a wrong answer.

slides.heading: Summary — Part 1
slides.body_md: Key results:

rows: P V = n R T = N k_B T (T in kelvin)
Boyle, Charles, Gay-Lussac and Avogadro follow
many tiny, elastic, non-interacting molecules, no preferred direction
mean translational energy (1/2) m v̄² = (3/2) k_B T

visual.alt: Summary table of the ideal gas equation, kinetic model, pressure, temperature and rms speed

slides.narration: To sum up. An ideal gas obeys pressure times volume equals n R T, in kelvin. The classical gas laws are special cases. The kinetic model, with many tiny, elastic, independent molecules, gives the pressure as one third of the density times the mean square speed. Comparing the two results shows that the kelvin temperature measures the mean translational kinetic energy, and fixes the root mean square speed.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 1
bullets: Always convert Celsius to kelvin before using P V = n R T; keep P in pascal and V in m³ when R = 8.314.
In derivations state the assumptions: elastic collisions, point molecules, no preferred direction.
v_rms is the root of the mean of the squares; v_rms ≥ mean speed.
Compare gases at one temperature by mean energy (equal) and by speed (not equal).

visual.alt: Table of partial pressures of two gases in a mixture and the total pressure by Dalton law

slides.narration: Convert Celsius to kelvin before using the gas equation, and keep pressure in pascals and volume in cubic metres when you use the gas constant eight point three one four. In a derivation, state the assumptions. Remember that the root mean square speed is at least as large as the mean speed. And at one temperature, different gases have the same mean energy but different speeds.

slides.narration: Molecules do more than fly in straight lines: a two atom molecule can also spin, and may even vibrate. In this part we count the ways a molecule can store energy, share the energy equally among them, and use that to explain the specific heats of gases. We finish with the distance a molecule travels between collisions, and with Avogadro's number.

slides.heading: Degrees of freedom
slides.body_md: The **degrees of freedom** of a molecule are the independent ways in which it can possess energy: translation, rotation, vibration.
bullets: **Monatomic** (He, Ar): 3 translational; no rotation of a point atom about its centre.
**Diatomic** (O₂, N₂): 3 translational + 2 rotational = 5; the spin about the bond axis does not count.
Non-linear **polyatomic** (H₂O, CH₄): 3 translational + 3 rotational = 6.
A vibrational mode stores both kinetic and potential energy, so it adds 2 quadratic terms; vibrations are active only at high temperatures.

slides.narration: A single atom can only move through space, so it has three degrees of freedom. A two atom molecule can also rotate about two axes perpendicular to the bond, giving five. A bent three atom molecule can rotate about three axes, giving six. Each vibration adds two more, one for its kinetic energy and one for its potential energy, but at ordinary temperatures vibrations are not excited.

slides.heading: The law of equipartition of energy
slides.body_md: In thermal equilibrium at temperature $T$ the total energy is shared equally among all the quadratic terms:
bullets: A molecule with $f$ quadratic terms has mean energy $\tfrac{f}{2} k_B T$; one mole has internal energy $U = \tfrac{f}{2} R T$.
For a monatomic gas the three translational terms give $\tfrac{3}{2} k_B T$, as found from kinetic theory.
Each vibrational mode counts twice, once for kinetic and once for potential energy.
For an ideal gas the internal energy depends only on the temperature.

rows: (f/2) k_B T per molecule, (f/2) R T per mole

visual.alt: Table of the energy per molecule for each kind of quadratic energy term by the law of equipartition

math: \text{energy per quadratic term} = \tfrac{1}{2} k_B T \text{ per molecule}
slides.narration: The law of equipartition says that in equilibrium every quadratic term in the energy of a molecule gets, on average, one half of k T. If a molecule has f such terms, its mean energy is f over two times k T, and one mole of gas has internal energy f over two times R T. A vibration counts twice, because it has both a kinetic and a potential term.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: energy stored in oxygen
slides.body_md: Oxygen at $330$ K (take $f = 5$) is in a closed cylinder. Find the mean energy of one molecule, the internal energy of one mole and of $2$ mol.
bullets: Per molecule: $\dfrac{f}{2} k_B T = 2.5 \times 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \times 330 = 1.14 \times 10^{-20}$ J.
Per mole: $\dfrac{f}{2} R T = 2.5 \times 8.314 \times 330 = 6859.1$ J.
For 2 mol: $U = 2 \times 6859.1 = 13718$ J $\approx 13.7$ kJ.

rows: Mean energy per molecule (5/2) k_B T
Internal energy per mole (5/2) R T

slides.narration: For oxygen treated as a rigid two atom molecule, there are five quadratic terms. The mean energy per molecule is five halves of k T, about one point one four times ten to the minus twenty joule. For one mole the internal energy is five halves of R T, near sixty nine hundred joules, so two moles hold about thirteen point seven kilojoules.

bullets: The relation $C_P - C_V = R$ for an ideal gas comes from the first law, as in the chapter on thermodynamics.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: heating nitrogen
slides.body_md: Nitrogen, a rigid diatomic gas ($f = 5$), $3$ mol, is heated through $40$ K. Find the heat needed at constant volume and at constant pressure, and the work done in the second case.
bullets: $Q_V = n C_V \Delta T = 3 \times 20.79 \times 40 = 2494.2$ J.
$Q_P = n C_P \Delta T = 3 \times 29.10 \times 40 = 3491.9$ J.
Work $= Q_P - Q_V = n R \Delta T = 997.68$ J, and $\gamma = 1.40$.

rows: Constant volume, Q = n C_V ΔT
Constant pressure, Q = n C_P ΔT
Difference = n R ΔT (work done by the gas)

slides.narration: For a rigid diatomic gas the molar specific heat at constant volume is five halves of R and at constant pressure seven halves of R. For three moles heated through forty kelvin, the constant volume heat is about twenty four hundred and ninety four joules, and the constant pressure heat is about thirty four hundred and ninety two joules. The difference, nine hundred and ninety eight joules, is the work done by the gas as it expands.

slides.heading: Specific heats of different gases
slides.body_md: Table of the predictions of the model; the number f depends on which modes are active.
bullets: Monatomic gases: $C_V = \tfrac{3}{2}R$, $\gamma = 5/3 \approx 1.667$.
Diatomic gases at ordinary temperatures behave as rigid (vibrations not excited): f = 5, γ = 7/5 = 1.4. At high temperature vibrations add 2 and γ falls to 9/7.
Non-linear polyatomic gases, rigid: $f = 6$, $C_V = 3R$, $C_P = 4R$, $\gamma = 4/3$. Each active vibrational mode adds $R$ to $C_V$.
For a mixture of gases, add the heat capacities of the parts, $C_V = \sum n_i C_{V,i}$ and $C_P = \sum n_i C_{P,i}$, then $\gamma = C_P/C_V$.

slides.heading: Worked example 8: a mixture of two gases
slides.body_md: A closed vessel holds $1$ mol of argon ($f = 3$) and $2$ mol of oxygen ($f = 5$, rigid). Find $\gamma$ for the mixture.

$C_P = (1 \times \tfrac{5}{2} + 2 \times \tfrac{7}{2}) R = 9.5 R$.
$\gamma = \dfrac{9.5}{6.5} = 1.46$, between 5/3 and 7/5.

slides.heading: Mean free path
slides.body_md: Molecules collide with each other. The average distance a molecule travels between two successive collisions is the **mean free path** $\lambda$.
bullets: The path of a molecule is a zigzag; the straight pieces have different lengths, and λ is their average.
For molecules of diameter $d$ and number density $n$: $\lambda = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}\,\pi d^2 n}$.
With $n = P/(k_B T)$: $\lambda = \dfrac{k_B T}{\sqrt{2}\,\pi d^2 P}$.
The collision frequency is about (average speed) $/\lambda$.

slides.narration: A molecule in a gas bumps into other molecules again and again, so its path is a zigzag of straight pieces of different lengths. The average length of these pieces is the mean free path. The bigger the molecules, or the more crowded they are, the shorter this distance. The number of collisions per second is the average speed divided by the mean free path.

slides.heading: What the mean free path depends on
slides.body_md: From $\lambda = 1/(\sqrt{2}\,\pi d^2 n)$ we can predict how it changes:
bullets: More molecules per unit volume (larger n) means more collisions, so a shorter λ.
Larger molecules (larger d) give a larger target, so a shorter λ; λ depends on d².
At fixed temperature λ ∝ 1/P: halving the pressure doubles λ.
Heating a gas in a sealed vessel does not change n and so does not change λ.

slides.narration: The mean free path falls when the gas is more crowded and when the molecules are larger, as the square of the diameter. At a fixed temperature it is inversely proportional to the pressure, so halving the pressure doubles it. But if you heat a gas in a sealed vessel, the number of molecules per unit volume does not change, and neither does the mean free path.

slides.body_md: Take nitrogen as molecules of diameter $3\times 10^{-10}$ m at $1.013 \times 10^5$ Pa and $300$ K, with mean speed about $470$ m s$^{-1}$. Find the mean free path and the collision frequency.
bullets: $\lambda = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}\,\pi d^2 n} = 1.02 \times 10^{-7}$ m, about $341$ times the molecular diameter.
Collisions per second $\approx \dfrac{470}{1.02 \times 10^{-7}} = 4.6 \times 10^{9}$ s$^{-1}$.

slides.heading: Avogadro's number and Avogadro's law
slides.body_md: One mole of any substance contains $N_A = 6.02 \times 10^{23}$ elementary units.
bullets: From $P V = N k_B T$: at the same $P$ and $T$, equal volumes of different gases contain the same number $N$ of molecules (**Avogadro\'s law**).

sections.heading: 1. Equation of state of a perfect gas
sections.body_md:
- An **ideal (perfect) gas** obeys $P V = n R T = N k_B T$ with $T$ in **kelvin** ($T = t_\text{C} + 273$). Here $n$ is the number of moles, $N = n N_A$ the number of molecules, $R = 8.314$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$, $k_B = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}$ J K$^{-1}$, $N_A = 6.02 \times 10^{23}$ mol$^{-1}$ and $R = N_A k_B$.
- **Special cases** for a fixed amount of gas: Boyle ($P V$ constant at fixed $T$; the P–V curves are hyperbolas called isotherms), Charles ($V/T$ constant at fixed $P$), Gay-Lussac ($P/T$ constant at fixed $V$), and the combined law $P_1 V_1/T_1 = P_2 V_2/T_2$. Avogadro's law: at the same $P$ and $T$, equal volumes of gases hold equal numbers of molecules.
- **Real gases** approach ideal behaviour at low pressure and high temperature; at high pressure the molecular volume matters and at low temperature the attractions matter, so the gas liquefies.
- Example: $4$ mol of helium in $0.05$ m$^3$ at 27 °C exerts $P = n R T/V = 2.00 \times 10^{5}$ Pa ($\approx 1.97$ atm). Dry air (M = 29 g mol$^{-1}$) at 1 atm and 300 K has density $PM/RT = 1.18$ kg m$^{-3}$, and one mole of it occupies $24.6$ litre.

A curve of constant temperature on a P–V graph; for an ideal gas it is the hyperbola P V = constant.

sections.heading: 2. Kinetic theory of an ideal gas: pressure, temperature and rms speed
sections.body_md:
- **Assumptions:** a large number of identical molecules in random motion; molecular size negligible compared with the separation; no forces except during collisions; elastic collisions with the walls and each other; no preferred direction and gravity ignored.
- **Pressure.** One molecule hitting a wall with $v_x$ gives it momentum $2 m v_x$; it returns after $2L/v_x$, so it exerts $m v_x^2/L$. Summing for $N$ molecules over a cube of volume $V = L^3$ and using $\overline{v_x^2} = \overline{v^2}/3$: $P = \tfrac{1}{3}\,\dfrac{N}{V}\,m\,\overline{v^2} = \tfrac{1}{3}\rho\,\overline{v^2}$. Equivalently $P V = \tfrac{2}{3}E$, where $E$ is the total translational kinetic energy.
- **Temperature.** Comparing with $P V = N k_B T$: $\tfrac{1}{2} m \overline{v^2} = \tfrac{3}{2} k_B T$. The kelvin temperature measures the mean translational kinetic energy per molecule, the same for every ideal gas. $v_\text{rms} = \sqrt{3 k_B T/m} = \sqrt{3 R T/M} \propto \sqrt{T}$, and for different gases at one temperature $v_\text{rms} \propto 1/\sqrt{M}$.
- The rms speed is never less than the mean speed. The mean velocity of the molecules is zero. In a mixture, each gas exerts its own partial pressure and the total is their sum (**Dalton's law**).
- Examples: hydrogen with $\rho = 0.09$ kg m$^{-3}$ and $v_\text{rms} = 1840$ m s$^{-1}$ has $P = 1.02 \times 10^{5}$ Pa. At 300 K nitrogen has $v_\text{rms} = 517$ m s$^{-1}$ and oxygen $484$ m s$^{-1}$, but each molecule has mean energy $6.21 \times 10^{-21}$ J. To raise $v_\text{rms}$ by a factor 1.5 from 27 °C one must go to $675$ K $= 402$ °C.

sections.heading: 3. Degrees of freedom, equipartition and specific heats
sections.body_md:
- **Degrees of freedom** are the independent ways a molecule can store energy. A monatomic molecule has 3 (translation); a rigid diatomic molecule 5 (3 translational and 2 rotational); a non-linear polyatomic molecule 6 (3 and 3). A vibrational mode stores kinetic and potential energy, so it adds 2 quadratic terms; vibrations are excited only at high temperatures, so a diatomic gas at room temperature behaves as rigid ($f = 5$) and at high temperature has $f = 7$.
- **Law of equipartition:** in equilibrium each quadratic term in the energy of a molecule has mean value $\tfrac{1}{2} k_B T$. With $f$ terms the energy per molecule is $\tfrac{f}{2} k_B T$ and the internal energy of $n$ moles of an ideal gas is $U = \tfrac{f}{2} n R T$.
- **Specific heats:** $C_V = \tfrac{f}{2} R$ and, because $C_P - C_V = R$ for an ideal gas (from the first law), $C_P = \left(\tfrac{f}{2} + 1\right) R$ and $\gamma = 1 + 2/f$. Monatomic: $\tfrac{3}{2}R$, $\tfrac{5}{2}R$, $5/3$. Rigid diatomic: $\tfrac{5}{2}R$, $\tfrac{7}{2}R$, $7/5$. Rigid non-linear polyatomic: $3R$, $4R$, $4/3$.
- For a mixture, $C_V = \sum n_i C_{V,i}$ and $C_P = \sum n_i C_{P,i}$ for the whole sample, then $\gamma = C_P/C_V$ (for 1.0 mol of argon and 2.0 mol of oxygen, $\gamma = 1.46$).
- Examples: oxygen at 330 K has $\tfrac{5}{2} k_B T = 1.14 \times 10^{-20}$ J per molecule and $U = 6859.1$ J per mole. Heating 3 mol of nitrogen by 40 K needs $2494.2$ J at constant volume and $3491.9$ J at constant pressure; the difference $n R \Delta T = 997.68$ J is the work done by the gas.

sections.heading: 4. Mean free path and Avogadro's number
sections.body_md:
- The **mean free path** $\lambda$ is the average distance a molecule travels between two successive collisions. For molecules of diameter $d$ and number density $n$, $\lambda = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}\,\pi d^2 n}$, and since $n = P/(k_B T)$, $\lambda = \dfrac{k_B T}{\sqrt{2}\,\pi d^2 P}$.
- Hence $\lambda$ is shorter for a more crowded gas and for larger molecules ($\lambda \propto 1/d^2$); at fixed $T$, $\lambda \propto 1/P$; at fixed $P$, $\lambda \propto T$; heating a gas in a sealed vessel leaves $n$, and so $\lambda$, unchanged. The collision frequency is about (mean speed)$/\lambda$.
- Example: nitrogen-like molecules ($d = 3.0 \times 10^{-10}$ m) at 1 atm and 300 K have $n = 2.45 \times 10^{25}$ m$^{-3}$ and $\lambda = 1.02 \times 10^{-7}$ m, about 341 diameters, and about $4.6 \times 10^{9}$ collisions per second at a mean speed of 470 m s$^{-1}$. At $0.01$ Pa $\lambda = 1.04$ m, longer than a 0.5 m tube.
- **Avogadro's number** $N_A = 6.02 \times 10^{23}$ mol$^{-1}$ is the number of molecules in one mole. The mass of a molecule is $M/N_A$, and $N = (m/M) N_A$ molecules are in a sample of mass $m$. From $P V = N k_B T$, equal volumes of any gases at the same $P$ and $T$ hold the same number of molecules (**Avogadro's law**). At 0 °C and 1 atm one mole occupies $22.4$ litre and the number density is $2.69 \times 10^{25}$ m$^{-3}$. For 2.8 g of nitrogen, $N = 6.02 \times 10^{22}$ and one molecule has mass $4.65 \times 10^{-26}$ kg.

- Say which modes are active before choosing f; then C_V = (f/2) R, C_P = C_V + R, γ = 1 + 2/f.
- Mean free path: sealed vessel, unchanged; fixed T, λ ∝ 1/P; fixed P, λ ∝ T; λ ∝ 1/d².

cards.front_md: Write the equation of state of an ideal gas in terms of moles and in terms of molecules.
cards.back_md: $P V = n R T = N k_B T$.

cards.front_md: Which temperature scale must be used in the gas equation?
cards.back_md: The absolute (kelvin) scale: $T = t_\text{C} + 273$.

cards.front_md: Value of the gas constant R used in this chapter?
cards.back_md: $8.314$ J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

cards.front_md: How are R, the Boltzmann constant and Avogadro's number related?
cards.back_md: $R = N_A k_B$, with $k_B = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}$ J K⁻¹ and $N_A = 6.02 \times 10^{23}$ mol⁻¹.

cards.front_md: What does Boyle's law say, and what is its graph at constant temperature?
cards.back_md: $P V$ is constant for a fixed amount of gas at fixed T; a hyperbola (isotherm).

cards.front_md: What is the V–T graph at constant pressure (kelvin scale)?
cards.back_md: A straight line through the origin: $V \propto T$ (Charles).

cards.front_md: Under what conditions does a real gas behave most like an ideal gas?
cards.back_md: Low pressure and high temperature.

cards.front_md: Show that density of an ideal gas is $\rho = P M / (R T)$.
cards.back_md: Put $n = m/M$ in $P V = n R T$ and divide by $V$.

cards.front_md: State two assumptions of the kinetic theory of an ideal gas.
cards.back_md: Any two: tiny molecules, no forces except in collisions, elastic collisions, random motion with no preferred direction.

cards.front_md: What is the momentum given to a wall by one elastic collision of a molecule with perpendicular speed $v_x$?
Pressure of an ideal gas in terms of density and mean square speed?
cards.back_md: $P = \tfrac{1}{3}\rho\,\overline{v^2}$.

cards.front_md: Why is $\overline{v_x^2} = \overline{v^2}/3$?
cards.back_md: No direction is preferred: $\overline{v_x^2} = \overline{v_y^2} = \overline{v_z^2}$ and they add up to $\overline{v^2}$.

cards.front_md: Mean translational kinetic energy per molecule at temperature T?
cards.back_md: $\tfrac{3}{2} k_B T$, whatever the gas.

cards.front_md: Write the rms speed in terms of T and molar mass.
cards.back_md: $v_\text{rms} = \sqrt{3 R T / M}$.

cards.front_md: How does the rms speed change if the temperature is quadrupled?
cards.back_md: It doubles ($\propto \sqrt{T}$).

cards.front_md: Two gases at the same temperature: which has the greater rms speed?
cards.back_md: The one with the smaller molar mass; their mean kinetic energies are equal.

cards.front_md: What is the mean velocity of the molecules of a gas at rest in a vessel?
cards.back_md: Zero; but the rms speed is not zero.

cards.front_md: State Dalton's law of partial pressures.
cards.back_md: The total pressure of a mixture of non-reacting gases is the sum of the pressures each would exert alone.

cards.front_md: How many degrees of freedom has a monatomic molecule? A rigid diatomic one?
cards.back_md: 3; 5 (3 translational + 2 rotational).

cards.front_md: How many degrees of freedom has a rigid non-linear polyatomic molecule?
cards.back_md: 6 (3 translational + 3 rotational), plus 2 for each active vibration.

cards.front_md: State the law of equipartition of energy.
cards.back_md: In equilibrium each quadratic term in the energy has mean value $\tfrac{1}{2} k_B T$ per molecule.

cards.front_md: Why does each vibrational mode count twice?
cards.back_md: It stores both kinetic and potential energy: two quadratic terms.

cards.front_md: Internal energy of n moles of an ideal gas with f degrees of freedom?
cards.back_md: $U = \tfrac{f}{2} n R T$.

cards.front_md: Give $C_V$ and $C_P$ in terms of f.
cards.back_md: $C_V = \tfrac{f}{2} R$ and $C_P = \left(\tfrac{f}{2} + 1\right) R$.

cards.front_md: What is $\gamma$ for a monatomic gas and for a rigid diatomic gas?
Define mean free path.
cards.back_md: The average distance a molecule travels between two successive collisions.

cards.front_md: Write the mean free path in terms of $n$ and $d$.
cards.back_md: $\lambda = 1 / (\sqrt{2}\,\pi d^2 n)$.

cards.front_md: A gas is heated in a sealed vessel. What happens to its mean free path?
cards.back_md: It is unchanged: n and d do not change.

cards.front_md: What does Avogadro's law say?
cards.back_md: Equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain the same number of molecules.

cards.front_md: Exam tip: how do you find the number of molecules in a sample of mass m?
cards.back_md: $N = (m/M) N_A$; the mass of one molecule is $M/N_A$.

questions.stem_md: A sample of 1 mol of an ideal gas is taken along two isotherms on a P–V graph, one at 300 K and one at 400 K. At the same volume, the pressure on the 400 K isotherm is

options.text_md: equal to it, because P V is constant for an ideal gas
4/3 times the pressure on the 300 K isotherm
less than it, because a hotter gas expands
greater than it by 100 kPa for every volume

questions.solution_md: At fixed n and V, P = nRT/V is proportional to T, so P(400)/P(300) = 400/300 = 4/3. P V is constant along one isotherm, not between two of them — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A fixed amount of an ideal gas has its volume halved while its absolute temperature is doubled. The pressure becomes

options.text_md: twice the original value
equal to the original value
four times the original value
one quarter of the original value

questions.solution_md: P = nRT/V, so P2/P1 = (T2/T1)(V1/V2) = 2 × 2 = 4 — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The volume of a fixed amount of gas is measured at constant pressure at several temperatures. A graph that is a straight line passing through the origin is obtained by plotting the volume against

options.text_md: the temperature on the kelvin scale
the temperature on the Celsius scale
the reciprocal of the kelvin temperature
the pressure of the gas

questions.solution_md: V = (nR/P) T, so V is proportional to the kelvin temperature. On the Celsius scale the line is straight but cuts the axis at −273 °C — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A chemical engineer in a fertiliser plant wants to treat ammonia vapour as an ideal gas. Which choice of conditions makes this approximation best?

options.text_md: High pressure and a temperature just above the boiling point
High pressure and a very low temperature
Low pressure and a temperature well above the boiling point
Low pressure and a temperature just above the boiling point

questions.solution_md: A real gas is closest to ideal when the molecules are far apart (low pressure) and move fast (high temperature), so that their size and attractions do not matter — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? In P V = n R T the temperature of a sample at 27 °C may be entered directly as T = 27 when P is in pascal, V in cubic metre and R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. T must be the absolute temperature: T = 27 + 273 = 300 K. Using 27 would make the pressure about eleven times too small.

questions.stem_md: Written for N molecules, the gas equation is P V = N k T, where k = R/N_A is a constant named after the Austrian physicist ___.
questions.solution_md: The constant is the **Boltzmann** constant, k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.

questions.stem_md: A steel cylinder of volume 20.0 L holds 2.5 mol of oxygen at 27 °C. Taking R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, find the pressure of the gas in kPa (3 significant figures).

marking_scheme.step: T = 300 K and V = 0.020 m³ (SI units)

questions.stem_md: A weather balloon of volume 25 m³ is filled with helium (molar mass 4.0 g mol⁻¹) at 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and 7 °C. Taking R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, find the mass of helium in kg (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $T = 7 + 273 = 280$ K. $n = \dfrac{P V}{R T} = \dfrac{1.0 \times 10^5 \times 25}{8.314 \times 280} = 1074$ mol. Mass $= n M = 1074 \times 4.0 \times 10^{-3} = 4.30$ kg.

questions.stem_md: The air in a bus tyre is at an absolute pressure of 220 kPa and 27 °C on a cool morning in Jaipur. After a long run the air is at 47 °C. Assuming the volume of the air does not change, find its new pressure in kPa.
questions.solution_md: At constant volume and amount, $\dfrac{P_1}{T_1} = \dfrac{P_2}{T_2}$ with $T_1 = 300$ K and $T_2 = 320$ K. $P_2 = 220 \times \dfrac{320}{300} = 235$ kPa.

marking_scheme.step: Kelvin temperatures 300 K and 320 K; P/T constant

questions.stem_md: Treating nitrogen (molar mass 28 g mol⁻¹) as an ideal gas at 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa and 300 K, find its density in kg m⁻³ (3 significant figures). Use R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
questions.solution_md: With $n = m/M$, $P V = \dfrac{m}{M} R T$, so $\rho = \dfrac{m}{V} = \dfrac{P M}{R T} = \dfrac{1.013 \times 10^5 \times 0.028}{8.314 \times 300} = 1.14$ kg m$^{-3}$.

marking_scheme.step: ρ = PM/RT from the gas equation with n = m/M

questions.stem_md: A welder's cylinder of volume 30 L holds oxygen (molar mass 32 g mol⁻¹) at 1.2 × 10⁶ Pa and 300 K. After some gas is used, the pressure falls to 0.80 × 10⁶ Pa at the same temperature. Find the mass of oxygen used, in g (3 significant figures; R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹).
questions.solution_md: At fixed $V$ and $T$, $n = \dfrac{P V}{R T}$, so the amount used is $\Delta n = \dfrac{(P_1 - P_2) V}{R T} = \dfrac{(1.2 - 0.80) \times 10^6 \times 0.030}{8.314 \times 300} = 4.811$ mol. Mass $= \Delta n \times 32$ g mol$^{-1}$ $= 154$ g.

marking_scheme.step: V = 0.030 m³; n = PV/RT before and after

questions.stem_md: An air bubble of volume 8.0 cm³ at the surface of a lake (pressure 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa) sinks to a depth of 15 m. Assuming the temperature of the air in the bubble does not change, find its volume at that depth in cm³. Take the density of water as 1000 kg m⁻³ and g = 9.8 m s⁻².
questions.solution_md: Pressure at depth: $P = P_0 + \rho g h = 1.013 \times 10^5 + 1000 \times 9.8 \times 15 = 248300$ Pa. At constant $T$ and $n$, $P_1 V_1 = P_2 V_2$, so $V_2 = 8.0 \times \dfrac{1.013 \times 10^5}{248300} = 3.26$ cm$^3$.

questions.stem_md: Show that Boyle's law and Charles' law follow from the ideal gas equation.

answer.model_answer_md: The ideal gas equation is **P V = n R T**. For a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature the right-hand side is constant, so **P V = constant** (Boyle). At constant pressure, **V/T = nR/P** is constant, so V is proportional to the absolute temperature (Charles).

questions.solution_md: PV = nRT: T fixed gives PV constant; P fixed gives V/T constant.

marking_scheme.step: Constant n and T: P V = nRT = constant (Boyle)
Constant n and P: V/T = nR/P = constant (Charles), T in kelvin

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons why a real gas deviates from ideal behaviour when it is compressed to a high pressure or cooled to a low temperature.

answer.model_answer_md: An ideal gas assumes point molecules with no mutual forces. At **high pressure** the molecules are crowded, so their own volume is no longer negligible compared with the container. At **low temperature** they move slowly, so the **attractive forces** between them matter and the gas may liquefy.

questions.solution_md: Finite size of molecules at high pressure; attractions at low temperature.

marking_scheme.step: High pressure: molecular volume not negligible

questions.stem_md: Describe the shape of the P–V graph of a fixed amount of an ideal gas at two temperatures T₁ < T₂ drawn on the same axes, and explain how the two curves are placed relative to each other.

answer.model_answer_md: Each curve is a **rectangular hyperbola** because P V = nRT is constant at constant temperature, so P falls as V increases and neither axis is cut. Each is called an **isotherm**. At any given volume the pressure P = nRT/V is proportional to T, so the T₂ curve lies **above** the T₁ curve everywhere, and the curves never cross.

questions.solution_md: Hyperbolas; hotter isotherm lies higher.

marking_scheme.step: Hyperbola: PV = nRT constant on one isotherm
P ∝ T at fixed V, so higher T gives the higher curve
Curves do not intersect; isotherms never cross

questions.stem_md: Which one of the following is NOT an assumption made in the kinetic theory of an ideal gas?

options.text_md: Collisions of the molecules with the walls of the vessel are elastic
The molecules attract one another with a force that increases as they come closer
The volume of the molecules is negligible compared with the volume of the container
The molecules move at random and no direction of motion is preferred

questions.solution_md: The model assumes no forces between molecules except during collisions. The other three statements are assumptions of the model — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A fixed number of molecules of an ideal gas is kept in a closed rigid vessel, and every molecule is made to move twice as fast. The pressure on the walls becomes

options.text_md: twice the original value
equal to the original value
four times the original value
one half of the original value

questions.solution_md: P = (1/3)(N/V) m v̄² with N, V and m fixed, so P is proportional to v̄². Doubling every speed multiplies v̄² by 4 — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The molecules of a gas in a closed vessel have a range of speeds. If v̄ is the mean speed and v_rms the root-mean-square speed, then

options.text_md: v_rms is always equal to v̄
v_rms is always less than v̄
v_rms is greater than v̄ unless all the molecules have the same speed
v_rms is zero because the molecules move in all directions

questions.solution_md: Squaring gives extra weight to the faster molecules, so the root of the mean of the squares is never less than the mean of the speeds; they are equal only if all speeds are equal. Velocities cancel in direction, speeds do not — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A gas is at rest in a closed cylinder on a table. The mean (vector) velocity of its molecules is

options.text_md: equal to the rms speed of the molecules
equal to the mean speed of the molecules
one third of the rms speed
zero, because the molecules move equally in all directions

questions.solution_md: For every molecule moving one way there is another moving the opposite way on average, so the vector sum of the velocities is zero (the speeds do not cancel) — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A sealed bottle contains a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen in thermal equilibrium at 300 K. Compared with an oxygen molecule, the mean translational kinetic energy of a hydrogen molecule is

options.text_md: equal
four times as large, since hydrogen molecules are four times as fast
sixteen times as large, since hydrogen is sixteen times lighter
one quarter as large, since hydrogen is lighter

questions.solution_md: The mean translational energy (3/2)k_B T depends only on temperature, not on the kind of molecule. Hydrogen is faster (by a factor 4) but lighter by the compensating factor 16 — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A gas in a sealed cylinder is heated from 27 °C to 54 °C. The rms speed of its molecules becomes about

options.text_md: 2 times the original value
1.41 times the original value
the same as the original value
1.04 times the original value

questions.solution_md: $v_\text{rms} \propto \sqrt{T}$ with $T$ in kelvin: $\sqrt{327/300} = 1.04$. Doubling the Celsius value does not double the kelvin temperature — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A gas in a closed vessel exerts a steady pressure on the walls even though each molecule strikes a wall only now and then.

**Reason (R):** The number of molecules is so large that their many small impacts every second average out to a steady force.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true and R explains A: pressure is the average momentum transferred per unit time and area by an enormous number of molecules — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** At 300 K the rms speed of hydrogen molecules is the same as that of oxygen molecules.

**Reason (R):** At a given temperature all ideal gas molecules have the same mean translational kinetic energy.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: R is true, but because the molar masses differ, v_rms = √(3RT/M) differs (hydrogen is 4 times faster than oxygen); A is false — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? At the same temperature, the rms speed of the molecules of the heavier of two ideal gases is smaller than that of the lighter one.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. v_rms = √(3RT/M) decreases as the molar mass M increases at a fixed temperature.

questions.stem_md: The square root of the average of the squares of the speeds of all the molecules of a gas is called its ___ speed.
questions.solution_md: It is the **root-mean-square** (rms) speed.

questions.stem_md: Argon (molar mass 40 g mol⁻¹) fills an electric bulb. Find the rms speed of its atoms at 27 °C, in m s⁻¹ (3 significant figures; R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹).
questions.solution_md: $v_\text{rms} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3 R T}{M}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3 \times 8.314 \times 300}{0.040}} = \sqrt{187065} = 433$ m s$^{-1}$.

marking_scheme.step: T = 300 K; v_rms = √(3RT/M) with M in kg

questions.stem_md: The escape speed from the Moon's surface is 2.4 × 10³ m s⁻¹. At what temperature would the rms speed of hydrogen molecules (molar mass 2.0 g mol⁻¹) equal this speed? Give the answer in K (3 significant figures; R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹).
questions.solution_md: $v_\text{rms}^2 = \dfrac{3 R T}{M}$, so $T = \dfrac{M v_\text{rms}^2}{3 R} = \dfrac{2.0 \times 10^{-3} \times (2400)^2}{3 \times 8.314} = \dfrac{11520}{24.942} = 462$ K.

marking_scheme.step: T = M v²/(3R) with M = 2.0 × 10⁻³ kg mol⁻¹

questions.stem_md: A vessel of volume 2.0 L contains 1.0 × 10²³ molecules of a gas, each of mass 5.0 × 10⁻²⁶ kg, with an rms speed of 400 m s⁻¹. Find the pressure of the gas in kPa (3 significant figures).

marking_scheme.step: P = N m v²/(3V), V in m³

questions.stem_md: Gas in the lungs of a healthy person is at body temperature, 37 °C. Find the mean translational kinetic energy of a molecule of an ideal gas at this temperature, in units of 10⁻²¹ J (3 significant figures; k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹).
At what temperature would the mean translational kinetic energy of a gas molecule equal 1.0 eV? Take 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J and k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹. Give the answer in K (3 significant figures).
A gas sealed in a flask at −23 °C is warmed until the rms speed of its molecules is 1.2 times its value at −23 °C. Find the new temperature in °C.
questions.solution_md: $T_1 = -23 + 273 = 250$ K. Since $v_\text{rms} \propto \sqrt{T}$, $T_2 = T_1 \times 1.2^2 = 250 \times 1.44 = 360$ K. In degrees Celsius $t_2 = 360 - 273 = 87$ °C.

questions.stem_md: A rigid vessel of volume 0.050 m³ at 27 °C holds a mixture of 2.0 mol of hydrogen and 3.0 mol of helium. Taking both as ideal gases and R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, find the total pressure of the mixture in kPa (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: Each gas fills the whole vessel. $P_1 = \dfrac{2.0 \times 8.314 \times 300}{0.050} = 99768$ Pa $= 99.77$ kPa and $P_2 = \dfrac{3.0 \times 8.314 \times 300}{0.050} = 149650$ Pa $= 149.7$ kPa. By Dalton's law $P = P_1 + P_2 = 249$ kPa.

marking_scheme.step: Partial pressures P₁ and P₂ from P = nRT/V

questions.stem_md: Five molecules of a gas have speeds of 300, 400, 500, 600 and 700 m s⁻¹. Find their root-mean-square speed in m s⁻¹ (3 significant figures).

marking_scheme.step: Mean of the squared speeds = 270 000 m² s⁻²

questions.stem_md: The molecules of a gas in a closed tank of volume 0.30 m³ have a total translational kinetic energy of 54 kJ. Find the pressure of the gas in kPa (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: From $P = \tfrac{1}{3}\dfrac{N m \overline{v^2}}{V}$ and $E = \tfrac{1}{2} N m \overline{v^2}$: $P = \dfrac{2E}{3V} = \dfrac{2 \times 54\,000}{3 \times 0.30} = 120000$ Pa $= 120$ kPa.

marking_scheme.step: P = 2E/(3V) from P = (1/3)N m v̄²/V and E = (1/2)N m v̄²

questions.stem_md: State four assumptions made in the kinetic theory of an ideal gas.

answer.model_answer_md: The gas consists of a very large number of identical **molecules in random motion**. The molecular volume is **negligible** compared with that of the container. There are **no forces** between molecules except during collisions. All collisions, with each other and with the walls, are **elastic**, and no direction is preferred.

questions.solution_md: Four of the listed assumptions.

questions.stem_md: Use the kinetic theory to explain why the pressure of a fixed mass of gas in a rigid closed vessel rises when the gas is heated.

answer.model_answer_md: Heating raises the **mean kinetic energy** of the molecules, so their rms speed increases. They then strike the walls **more often** and each impact transfers **more momentum**. The force per unit area, the pressure, therefore increases, since P is proportional to v̄² when N and V are fixed.

questions.solution_md: Higher speed: more frequent, harder collisions.

marking_scheme.step: Higher temperature gives higher mean kinetic energy and speed
More frequent impacts with more momentum each, so P rises

questions.stem_md: The mean velocity of the molecules of a gas at rest in a closed box is zero, yet their rms speed is not. Explain how both statements can be true.

answer.model_answer_md: Velocity is a **vector**: with no preferred direction, the velocities of the molecules cancel in pairs, so the average velocity is **zero**. The rms speed uses the **squares** of the speeds, which are positive whatever the direction, so their average, and its root, is not zero.

questions.solution_md: Vector cancellation versus positive squares.

marking_scheme.step: Velocities cancel by direction: mean velocity zero
Squares are positive, so rms speed is not zero

questions.stem_md: Explain why, at the same temperature, hydrogen molecules move faster than oxygen molecules, even though both have the same mean translational kinetic energy. Find the ratio of their rms speeds (molar masses 2.0 and 32 g mol⁻¹).

answer.model_answer_md: The mean translational kinetic energy $\tfrac{1}{2} m \overline{v^2} = \tfrac{3}{2} k_B T$ is the **same for every ideal gas** at temperature $T$, whatever the mass of its molecules. To carry the same energy, a **lighter** molecule must move faster, because the rms speed $\sqrt{3RT/M}$ varies as $1/\sqrt{M}$. For hydrogen and oxygen the ratio is $\dfrac{v_{H}}{v_{O}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{32}{2.0}} = 4$, so hydrogen molecules are four times as fast as oxygen molecules.

questions.solution_md: Same energy, smaller mass, larger speed; ratio 4.

marking_scheme.step: Same mean KE (3/2)k_B T for all gases at T

questions.stem_md: Three molecules of a gas have speeds of 300, 400 and 800 m s⁻¹. Find their mean speed and rms speed, and say which is larger and why.

answer.model_answer_md: The mean speed is the sum of the speeds divided by the number of molecules: $\dfrac{300 + 400 + 800}{3} = 500$ m s$^{-1}$. For the rms speed, square each speed, take the mean of the squares, $\dfrac{9 + 16 + 64}{3} \times 10^4 = 296667$ m$^2$ s$^{-2}$, and then take the square root: $v_\text{rms} = 545$ m s$^{-1}$. The rms speed is the larger of the two, because squaring gives more weight to the fastest molecule.

questions.solution_md: Mean 500, rms 545.

marking_scheme.step: rms exceeds mean: squaring weights fast molecules more

questions.stem_md: State Dalton's law of partial pressures and use the kinetic theory to justify it for two ideal gases mixed in one vessel.

answer.model_answer_md: **Dalton's law:** the total pressure of a mixture of non-reacting gases is the **sum of the partial pressures**, each being the pressure that gas would exert if it alone filled the vessel. In the kinetic picture the molecules do not interact, so each kind strikes the walls independently with $P_1 = \tfrac{1}{3}(N_1/V) m_1 \overline{v_1^2}$ and $P_2$ likewise. The wall feels the **sum** of the two momentum transfers, so $P = P_1 + P_2$.

questions.solution_md: Independent molecules; impacts add.

marking_scheme.step: Molecules do not interact: each gas strikes the walls independently
Momentum transfers add: P = P₁ + P₂

questions.stem_md: A rigid closed vessel holds neon, a monatomic gas, at room temperature. By the law of equipartition its molar heat capacity at constant volume is

options.text_md: 5R/2, because a neon atom can rotate about two axes
3R/2, because only the three translational terms store energy
3R, because each atom has three kinetic and three potential terms
R, because the gas does work as it is heated

questions.solution_md: A point-like atom has three translational degrees of freedom, each with ½k_BT, so U = (3/2)RT per mole and C_V = 3R/2 — option (b).

questions.stem_md: At a very high temperature the vibrational motion of a diatomic gas is also excited, so that each molecule has 7 degrees of freedom. For this gas the ratio C_P/C_V is
questions.solution_md: $\gamma = 1 + \dfrac{2}{f} = 1 + \dfrac{2}{7} = \dfrac{9}{7}$ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The law of equipartition of energy states that, for a gas in thermal equilibrium at absolute temperature T, the mean energy associated with each quadratic term in the energy of a molecule is

options.text_md: ½ k_B T
k_B T
½ R T

questions.solution_md: Each quadratic term (translation, rotation, or each of the kinetic and potential parts of a vibration) has mean value ½k_BT per molecule. ½RT is the value per mole — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Oxygen at room temperature is found to behave as a gas with 5 and not 7 degrees of freedom. The reason is that

options.text_md: an oxygen molecule cannot rotate about any axis
the vibrational motion is not excited at ordinary temperatures, so it adds nothing to the energy
the rotational motion about the bond is excited but not about the other axes
the law of equipartition holds only for monatomic gases

questions.solution_md: At room temperature the thermal energy is too small to excite the vibrations of a diatomic molecule, so only 3 translational and 2 rotational terms count. At high temperature f becomes 7 — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Treating nitrogen at room temperature as a rigid diatomic ideal gas, the internal energy of one mole at absolute temperature T is

questions.stem_md: Using the law of equipartition, obtain C_V, C_P and γ for a monatomic gas and for a rigid diatomic gas.

answer.model_answer_md: By equipartition each of the $f$ quadratic terms of a molecule carries $\tfrac{1}{2} k_B T$, so one mole has internal energy $U = \tfrac{f}{2} R T$ and the heat capacity at constant volume is $C_V = \tfrac{f}{2} R$. At constant pressure the gas also does work, and $C_P = C_V + R$, so $\gamma = 1 + 2/f$. A **monatomic** gas has $f = 3$: $C_V = \tfrac{3}{2}R$, $C_P = \tfrac{5}{2}R$, $\gamma = \tfrac{5}{3}$. A **rigid diatomic** gas has $f = 5$: $C_V = \tfrac{5}{2}R$, $C_P = \tfrac{7}{2}R$, $\gamma = \tfrac{7}{5}$.

questions.stem_md: Write the formula for the mean free path of a gas of molecules of diameter d at number density n, and state how it changes if (a) d is doubled, (b) the pressure is halved at constant temperature, (c) the gas is heated in a sealed rigid vessel.

(a) Since $\lambda \propto 1/d^2$, doubling the diameter makes the mean free path **one quarter** of its value. (b) At constant temperature the number density $n$ is proportional to the pressure, so halving the pressure **doubles** the mean free path. (c) In a sealed rigid vessel neither $n$ nor $d$ changes, so the mean free path is **unchanged**.

A mole is the amount of substance that contains Avogadro's number of molecules, so a mole has a mass in grams equal to its molar mass.

questions.stem_md: (a) State four assumptions of the kinetic theory of an ideal gas. (b) Derive the expression P = (1/3) ρ v̄² for the pressure of an ideal gas in a cube of side L, by considering the collisions of its molecules with one wall. (c) An enclosure holds a gas of density 1.2 kg m⁻³ whose molecules have an rms speed of 500 m s⁻¹. Find its pressure in kPa.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Many identical molecules in random motion; molecular volume negligible; no forces except in collisions; elastic collisions; no preferred direction.

(b) Take a molecule of mass $m$ with velocity component $v_x$ towards a wall. After an elastic collision the component is $-v_x$, so the wall gets momentum $2 m v_x$. The molecule returns after $2L/v_x$, so the force it exerts on average is $\dfrac{2 m v_x}{2L/v_x} = \dfrac{m v_x^2}{L}$. For $N$ molecules the pressure on the wall of area $L^2$ is $P = \dfrac{m}{L^3}\left(v_{x1}^2 + \cdots + v_{xN}^2\right) = \dfrac{N m \overline{v_x^2}}{V}$. With no preferred direction, $\overline{v_x^2} = \dfrac{\overline{v^2}}{3}$, so $P = \dfrac{1}{3}\dfrac{N m}{V}\overline{v^2} = \dfrac{1}{3}\rho\,\overline{v^2}$.

(c) $P = \dfrac{1}{3} \times 1.2 \times 500^2 = 100000$ Pa $= 100$ kPa.

questions.solution_md: Assumptions; derivation; 100 kPa.

marking_scheme.step: Any four assumptions of the model
Momentum change 2 m v_x per collision and time 2L/v_x between collisions: force m v_x²/L
Sum over N molecules: P = N m v̄_x²/V
Use of v̄_x² = v̄²/3 to reach P = (1/3)ρ v̄²

questions.stem_md: (a) Using P = (1/3) ρ v̄² and the equation of state, show that the mean translational kinetic energy of a molecule of an ideal gas is (3/2) k_B T. (d) At what temperature, in °C, would hydrogen (molar mass 2.0 g mol⁻¹) have the same rms speed as helium at 27 °C? Use R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) For $N$ molecules $P V = \tfrac{1}{3} N m \overline{v^2}$, and also $P V = N k_B T$. Equating, $\tfrac{1}{3} m \overline{v^2} = k_B T$, so $\tfrac{1}{2} m \overline{v^2} = \tfrac{3}{2} k_B T$, which depends only on the temperature.

(b) $v_\text{rms} = \sqrt{\overline{v^2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3 k_B T}{m}}$; with $m = M/N_A$ and $R = N_A k_B$ this is $\sqrt{\dfrac{3 R T}{M}}$.

(c) $T = 300$ K, so $v_\text{rms} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3 \times 8.314 \times 300}{4.0 \times 10^{-3}}} = 1368$ m s$^{-1}$.

(d) Equal speeds need $T/M$ equal, so $T_H = 300 \times \dfrac{2.0}{4.0} = 150$ K $= -123\,^\circ$C.

marking_scheme.step: Equating (1/3)N m v̄² to N k_B T

(a) In thermal equilibrium at temperature $T$ the energy is shared equally among the quadratic terms: each has a mean value $\tfrac{1}{2} k_B T$ per molecule.

(b) Monatomic: $f = 3$; rigid diatomic: $f = 5$ (3 translational + 2 rotational); rigid non-linear polyatomic: $f = 6$ (3 + 3).

(d) $N = n N_A = 0.2 \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} = 1.20 \times 10^{23}$.

questions.passage_md: The Moon has no atmosphere. At midday on the lunar surface the temperature of the ground and of any gas near it is about 380 K. The escape speed from the Moon is 2.4 × 10³ m s⁻¹. A mission planner compares hydrogen (molar mass 2.0 g mol⁻¹) with nitrogen (molar mass 28 g mol⁻¹) as gases that might be released near the lander. Take R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (a) larger than that of nitrogen molecules, because hydrogen molecules are lighter

**(b)** 2180 m/s

**(c)** (i) $\dfrac{v_H}{v_N} = \sqrt{\dfrac{M_N}{M_H}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{28}{2.0}} = 3.74$. Hydrogen molecules are about 3.7 times faster, so far more of them reach the escape speed; **hydrogen** is the gas more easily lost.

**OR** (ii) The claim is **wrong**. Equal temperature means equal mean **kinetic energy**, not equal speed. $v_\text{rms}$ varies as $1/\sqrt{M}$, so for nitrogen $v_\text{rms} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3 \times 8.314 \times 380}{0.028}} = 582$ m s$^{-1}$, about a quarter of the speed of hydrogen.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** v_rms = √(3RT/M) varies as 1/√M at one temperature. The mean translational kinetic energy is the same for both gases — option (a).

**(b)** $v_\text{rms} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3 R T}{M}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3 \times 8.314 \times 380}{2.0 \times 10^{-3}}} = \sqrt{4738980} = 2180$ m s$^{-1}$.

**(c)** (i) √14 = 3.74; hydrogen.

(ii) Nitrogen is about 582 m/s.

questions.passage_md: In a laboratory in Bengaluru a student heats a gas in a rigid sealed bulb and finds that its molar heat capacity at constant volume is 20.8 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. She treats the gas as ideal. Use R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (c) a diatomic gas with 5 active degrees of freedom

**(b)** 29.1 J/(mol K)

**(c)** (i) At constant pressure the heat needed is $Q = n C_P \Delta T = 2 \times 29.114 \times 30 = 1746.8$ J $= 1.75$ kJ. This is more than the heat needed at constant volume for the same rise in temperature, because the gas also does work of expansion against the surroundings.

**OR** (ii) The suggestion is **wrong**. Helium is a monatomic gas with only three degrees of freedom ($f = 3$), so its molar heat capacity at constant volume would be $C_V = \tfrac{3}{2}R = 12.47$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$, much less than the measured $20.8$. The measured value is very close to $\tfrac{5}{2}R = 20.79$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$, which points to a rigid diatomic gas with $f = 5$.

questions.passage_md: A vacuum chamber used to test a satellite instrument is a cube of side 2.0 m. It is filled with helium atoms (diameter 2.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m) at a pressure of 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ Pa and a temperature of 300 K. Take k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (b) the walls of the chamber, because the mean free path is larger than the chamber

**(b)** 46.6 m

**(c)** (i) At constant $T$, $\lambda \propto 1/P$, so $P_2 = P \dfrac{\lambda}{\lambda_2} = 5.0 \times 10^{-4} \times \dfrac{46.6}{2.0} = 0.0116$ Pa. At a higher pressure than this, atoms would collide with each other more often than with the walls.

**OR** (ii) The claim is **wrong**. In a sealed chamber the number of atoms per unit volume $n$ and the atomic diameter $d$ do not change, and $\lambda = 1/(\sqrt{2}\,\pi d^2 n)$ depends only on these, so $\lambda$ is **unchanged** at 46.6 m. The pressure doubles and the atoms collide more often because they are faster, but they still travel the same average distance between collisions.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** λ is much larger than 2.0 m (about 47 m), so an atom crosses the chamber far more often than it meets another atom: collisions are mostly with the walls — option (b).

**(b)** $n = \dfrac{P}{k_B T} = \dfrac{5.0 \times 10^{-4}}{1.38 \times 10^{-23} \times 300} = 1.21 \times 10^{17}$ m$^{-3}$. $\lambda = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}\,\pi d^2 n} = \dfrac{1}{1.414 \times 3.142 \times (2.0 \times 10^{-10})^2 \times 1.21 \times 10^{17}} = 46.6$ m.

**(c)** (i) P ∝ 1/λ; about 0.0116 Pa.

(ii) λ unchanged in a sealed chamber.
